item.title: US FDA grants tentative nod to Dr Reddy's twice-yearly HIV prevention drug
item.description: The tentative approval for generic lenacapavir is expected to accelerate affordable access to the twice-yearly HIV prevention injection across 120 countries outside the US.
item.dc:creator: Anjali Singh
item.content:encoded: Dr Reddy’s Laboratories has received tentative approval from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for its generic version of lenacapavir, a long-acting injectable drug administered twice a year to prevent HIV infection. The approval is expected to accelerate access to the drug across 120 countries outside the US under a voluntary licensing agreement with its innovator, Gilead Sciences. The approval has been granted under the FDA’s President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) programme. Under an existing agreement with Unitaid, the Wits Reproductive Health and HIV Institute (Wits RHI) and the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI), the injectable is expected to be made available at $40 per person annually across the 120 countries covered by Gilead’s voluntary licence. The first supplies are expected to reach countries before the end of 2026, with a broader rollout across eligible markets in 2027, the company said on Monday. The development follows a voluntary licence granted by Gilead to Dr Reddy’s in October 2024. In September 2025, the Hyderabad-based drugmaker entered into an agreement with Unitaid, Wits RHI and CHAI to support product development, expedite regulatory approvals and facilitate affordable access to the drug. Lenacapavir offers an alternative to existing pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) options, which often require more frequent administration. Given twice a year, the long-acting injectable is intended to reduce the risk of sexually acquired HIV-1 in adults and adolescents weighing at least 35 kg. “This is a moment of immense pride for all of us at Dr Reddy’s. Developing and manufacturing a complex long-acting injectable like lenacapavir at an affordable price required strong scientific capabilities and manufacturing expertise to address an urgent access need,” said Deepak Sapra, chief executive officer, API and Services, Dr Reddy’s Laboratories. The FDA's tentative approval marks a significant regulatory milestone, although wider availability will also depend on further steps, including World Health Organization (WHO) prequalification and national regulatory approvals in individual markets. The approval comes amid efforts to expand access to long-acting HIV prevention options, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, where daily medication can pose challenges to adherence and uptake. Unitaid said its support had helped accelerate the timeline for generic lenacapavir, bringing the approval process closer to the originator's launch rather than the decade-long gap often seen in generic drug development. “Now, with lenacapavir, we have helped shorten that timeline to just over a year. For young women in Africa, this translates into faster access to a groundbreaking HIV prevention option,” said Philippe Duneton, executive director of Unitaid. The WHO has also recommended twice-yearly lenacapavir in its HIV prevention guidelines. However, health systems will need to prepare for its introduction through provider training, community engagement and wider delivery infrastructure, Wits RHI said. Dr Reddy’s said the development strengthens its public health access portfolio and demonstrates its capabilities in developing and manufacturing complex medicines. The company is working with its partners to support product introduction and generate real-world evidence to guide its rollout across underserved populations.

item.title: What's inside China's 18-point plan to protect workers from AI job losses?
item.description: The State Council guidelines call for employment-risk assessments of AI projects, advance notice to affected workers, retraining support and stronger labour protections as businesses adopt AI ...
item.dc:creator: Apexa Rai
item.content:encoded: China has issued an 18-point plan to protect workers from job displacement caused by artificial intelligence (AI), asking companies to assess the employment impact of AI adoption, provide advance notice to affected employees and support workers in transitioning to new roles. The guidelines, issued by the General Office of China's State Council, seek to make the country's development model more employment-friendly as businesses increasingly adopt AI technologies, Reuters reported.  The guidelines outline measures across six areas - creating jobs through AI, making AI adoption more employment-friendly, improving workers' digital skills, strengthening employment services, protecting labour rights and monitoring employment risks.What does China's 18-point AI employment plan propose?One key proposal is to encourage companies to establish an 'unemployment buffer period' when introducing AI on a large scale. During this period, businesses are encouraged to inform affected employees in advance and provide support for retraining, transfers to other roles and finding alternative employment. The guidelines also call for employment-risk assessments of AI projects in areas subject to market-access requirements if their implementation could significantly affect jobs. Relevant departments are expected to coordinate support for workers facing displacement. China has also called for a cautious approach to AI adoption in labour-intensive industries, with authorities asked to consider the scale, intensity and pace of deployment to minimise the impact on workers. At the same time, AI applications are to be prioritised in jobs facing labour shortages or hazardous working conditions, where the technology can improve workplace safety and efficiency.Focus on retraining and new job opportunitiesThe plan seeks to expand employment opportunities in the AI sector while helping workers adapt to changing skill requirements. Universities and vocational institutions are encouraged to update their courses, introduce more AI-related specialisations and work with businesses to develop training programmes. The guidelines propose specialised AI training for university graduates, young people, migrant workers and unemployed people. Public training centres and businesses are also expected to play a role in improving workers' digital skills. Workers affected by AI-related job displacement are to receive targeted career guidance, skills training, job recommendations and support for starting businesses. Eligible unemployed workers should also receive unemployment insurance benefits. The government has further proposed using AI to improve employment services, including job-matching platforms, recruitment services and the delivery of employment-related benefits.Labour rights and social security protectionsThe 18-point plan also addresses concerns about workers' rights in workplaces increasingly shaped by human-machine collaboration. It calls on businesses to protect employees' rights to wages, rest, leave and workplace safety. The government also plans to regulate the use of AI in human-resource management and address employment discrimination, fraudulent recruitment and privacy violations arising from the misuse of algorithms. The guidelines propose improving social security coverage for people in flexible employment and new forms of work. They also call for adjustments to income-distribution mechanisms so that workers can benefit from the economic gains generated by AI.Monitoring AI-related employment risksChina plans to strengthen the monitoring and early warning of employment risks associated with AI adoption. Government departments are expected to share industry and employment data and develop systems to track changes in job creation, job displacement and skill requirements. The guidelines also call for including AI-related employment risks in existing mechanisms for preventing and responding to large-scale unemployment, alongside contingency planning and coordination among relevant authorities.Why has China introduced the plan?The measures come as AI adoption expands across China's economy, raising questions about how technological advancement could affect employment. According to official figures cited by Xinhua, China's core AI industry was valued at more than 1.2 trillion yuan ($178.62 billion) in 2025, with more than 6,200 AI companies operating nationwide. More than 30 per cent of manufacturing enterprises with annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan had adopted AI technologies by the end of 2025.

item.title: Sebi cuts OFS cooling-off for privately listed illiquid InvITs to 8 weeks
item.description: Sebi has shortened the cooling-off period for offer-for-sale transactions by privately listed illiquid InvITs to eight weeks from 12 weeks, effective immediately.
item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / News / Sebi cuts cool-off period for OFS by off-market illiquid Invits to 8 weeks

Sebi cuts cool-off period for OFS by off-market illiquid Invits to 8 weeks Sebi has shortened the cooling-off period for offer-for-sale transactions by privately listed illiquid InvITs to eight weeks from 12 weeks, effective immediately.

Sebi has reduced the cooling-off period for offer-for-sale transactions by privately listed illiquid infrastructure investment trusts to eight weeks from 12 weeks, aiming to ease trading-related restrictions. | Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India 1 min read Last Updated : Nov 02 2026 | 10:46 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Markets regulator Sebi on Monday reduced the cooling-off period for offer-for-sale (OFS) transactions by privately placed illiquid infrastructure investment trusts (InvITs) to 8 weeks from 12 weeks earlier.   At present, the cooling-off period for transactions â€“ purchases or sales before and after an OFS â€“ is based on liquidity. It stands at two weeks for the most liquid shares, four weeks for liquid shares and 12 weeks for illiquid shares.   Privately listed InvITs face inherent liquidity constraints due to their high trading lot size, which limits participation largely to institutional investors, body corporates and high-net-worth individuals. Consequently, trading volumes in such InvITs tend to remain thin and they may fall under the illiquid category because of these structural liquidity constraints.

"Based on the feedback received from market participants and in order to facilitate ease of doing business, it has been decided to reduce the cooling off period for illiquid private listed InvITs. The cooling off period in case of private listed InvITs whose units are illiquid shall be Â±8 weeks," the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) said in its circular.   This will come into force with immediate effect, according to Sebi.

item.title: Why Tesla, Samsung are pushing back against new US tariffs on Vietnam
item.description: Vietnamese goods currently face a 12.5 per cent US tariff, imposed in July over concerns that the country failed to stop imports of goods made using forced labour ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Why Tesla, Samsung are pushing back against new US tariffs on Vietnam

Why Tesla, Samsung are pushing back against new US tariffs on Vietnam Vietnamese goods currently face a 12.5 per cent US tariff, imposed in July over concerns that the country failed to stop imports of goods made using forced labour

Tesla has raised concerns that additional duties could make it harder for US companies to source products and components from Vietnam. (Image: Bloomberg)

Rimjhim Singh New Delhi 5 min read Last Updated : Nov 02 2026 | 11:57 AM IST

Listen to This Article

US businesses are divided over fresh tariffs on goods from Vietnam. While companies such as Tesla and Samsung oppose additional duties, several American industry groups want the government to impose penalties on Vietnam, news agency Reuters reported.   This comes as the Donald Trump administration approaches a November 29 deadline to complete an investigation into Vietnam's alleged intellectual property (IP) violations. The investigation, launched in May this year, could lead to new trade measures against the country.   According to submissions made to the US government and reviewed by Reuters , companies with manufacturing operations in Vietnam have warned that additional tariffs could disrupt their supply chains. On the other hand, groups representing American producers of steel, seafood, solar panels and other products have accused Vietnam of unfair trade practices and sought stronger action.

US tariffs on Vietnam: What is the dispute about?   The US Trade Representative (USTR) launched a trade investigation in May into Vietnam's alleged failure to protect intellectual property rights. Washington has accused the country of "a persistent failure to resolve long-standing concerns about IP protection and enforcement".   ALSO READ:  Bangladesh garment unrest shuts 529 factories, puts export orders at risk

The Trump administration has also designated Vietnam as a "priority foreign country", making it the first jurisdiction in 13 years to be placed in the most serious category of the US intellectual property watchlist.   A separate US investigation into Vietnam's alleged excess manufacturing capacity is also underway. Hanoi has urged Washington to ensure that its investigations are conducted objectively, Reuters reported.

Currently, Vietnamese goods face a general 12.5 per cent US tariff, imposed in July following an investigation into alleged failures to prevent imports of goods produced using forced labour.   Vietnam had earlier faced 20 per cent tariffs announced by Trump on what he called "Liberation Day". These duties were later struck down by the US Supreme Court. According to Reuters , economists believe the administration may seek to restore at least the same level of tariffs that were overturned.   Why Tesla and Samsung are opposing fresh tariffs   Tesla and Samsung have raised concerns that additional duties could make it harder for American companies to source products and components from Vietnam, affecting manufacturing operations in the US.

Tesla, in its submission to the USTR on July 2, asked the administration to "take into account the supply chain needs of American manufacturers".   The electric vehicle maker said that certain advanced components and precision manufacturing equipment were not available from domestic suppliers, despite significant investments in manufacturing within the US. This makes imports from countries such as Vietnam important for its operations.   Samsung's US subsidiary has expressed similar concerns. Vietnam accounts for a substantial share of the South Korean company's smartphone and network equipment production for the American market.   Samsung is also Vietnam's largest foreign investor, with investments of around $25 billion in the country, according to Reuters . Additional tariffs could affect its manufacturing operations and the movement of products from Vietnam to the US.

Other American businesses have also opposed fresh duties. Retail groups and trade associations representing companies in the footwear, apparel, bicycle and video game console industries have warned against additional tariffs because of their manufacturing links with Vietnam, the news report said.   US industry groups seek action against Vietnam   While companies such as Tesla and Samsung want Washington to avoid additional duties, several US industry groups have called for tougher action against Vietnam.   Trade associations representing American steel, seafood, plywood, solar panel and wood product manufacturers have accused Vietnam of following unfair trade practices. They have urged the US government to impose new tariffs to protect domestic producers.

Groups representing software, film and music companies have separately raised concerns about intellectual property protection and online piracy in Vietnam, the news report said.   The Business Software Alliance, which represents companies such as Microsoft, Oracle and IBM, has criticised Vietnam's enforcement of intellectual property laws. Citing a 2017 survey, the organisation said around three-fourths of the software installed on personal computers in Vietnam was unlicensed.   It also described Vietnam's enforcement efforts as "inadequate", despite repeated commitments by the country's government to address the issue.   The Motion Picture Association has also alleged that Vietnam is a major centre for online piracy. It said websites hosted in the country distribute illegally copied films and television programmes and attracted more than 12.5 billion visits worldwide last year.

The association has called for stronger action against piracy and better market access for legitimate streaming services.   Vietnam's growing trade ties with the US   The disagreement comes as Vietnam's exports to the US continue to rise. Its shipments to the American market increased 42 per cent in the first eight months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, making it the US' largest trading partner by goods surplus, ahead of China and Mexico, Reuters reported.   Vietnam was the US' fourth-largest trading partner by goods surplus at the end of 2025.   The growing trade relationship has made Vietnam an important manufacturing and sourcing base for American businesses. Any additional tariffs could therefore affect companies that depend on Vietnamese factories, while US producers are seeking protection against what they describe as unfair competition.
